newsitem.title: USA: Canceled timber sales could cost U.S. $300 million.
newsitem.headline: Canceled timber sales could cost U.S. $300 million.

text.p: Timber sales cancelled by the Clinton administration to protect nature could cost the government more than $300 million, according to a Congressional watchdog report released Thursday.

The Forest Service faced pending claims for $61 million and potential future claims of $198 million, while the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) faced claims for $2.2 million, with potential future claims of up to $42 million for cancelled or suspended sales, said the General Accounting Office report.
The General Accounting Office said the estimates of government exposure were uncertain and compensation awarded in future litigation could be "more or less."

Idaho Republican Sen. Larry Craig, chairman of the Senate forest panel who requested and released the report, warned that money might have to be diverted from other national forest programmes to pay the claims.

"Timber management officials are concerned that a large judgment against one or several forests could cause the Forest Service to stop all or some programmes in the forests or request supplemental appropriations to pay the damages," the report said.
Unlike the Bureau of Land Management, the Forest Service has yet to approve a revised timber sale contract that would limit its liability for cancelled sales, the report said.

"We recommend that the Secretary of Agriculture direct the Chief of the Forest Service to expeditiously release for public comment proposed regulations for cancelling timber sale contracts and a revised timber sale contract," GAO said.
The report said Forest Service officials in the Northwest had considered other ways to fund future damages, including establishing credits for the contract buyer to use for future timber sales.
